case_study_insert.main_stem: Thornwick Grange Inn (TGI) is a sole trader in the heritage inn and hospitality sector, employing a workforce of 23. Founded in 1998 by Margaret Thornwick, the business is a 16th-century coaching inn with restaurant and bar, and uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. TGI plans to invest $720,000 to restore the coach house into 10 en-suite guest rooms, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $270,000 of personal savings. It has fixed costs of $150,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $37, and currently produces 16,000 units a year. TGI faces two operational problems: service-quality complaints have risen and absenteeism among kitchen staff is 8%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — September 2026: A survey of 650 visitors found 72% chose Thornwick Grange for its historic character, 65% would pay a $18 premium for a coach-house room, and 54% dine in the inn restaurant during every stay. Average room rate last quarter was $88 with occupancy of 61%, up from 54% a year ago. Service complaints rose from 12 to 19 per month. Lead time for the coach-house booking diary is 8.5 weeks. A skills audit found 9 of 23 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the refurbished kitchen equipment; off-the-job courses at the culinary college cost $650 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Thornwick Grange Inn as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.8% to 5.5%, increasing mortgage and small-business loan costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.00 to $12.66 per hour from April 2026. (3) Utilities and energy costs have risen 13.1% year-on-year and hospitality food-cost inflation stands at 8.8%, while heritage-tourism visits grew 4.4% and domestic weekend-break demand rose 6.1%.

questions.question_text: TGI plans to finance part of the coach-house restoration with a $450,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for TGI of using personal savings to fund the expansion instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Personal savings carry no interest or repayment schedule, protecting the inn's cash flow while the coach house is restored and before the ten new rooms generate their share of revenue. With the base rate now at 5.5%, enlarging the loan would add interest on top of fixed costs of $150,000 a year and squeeze the $15 contribution earned on each of the 16,000 units sold — one-third of which are restaurant covers already priced against tight 8.8% food-cost inflation.

Point 2: Personal savings keep Margaret Thornwick fully in control without lender covenants over a historic listed building — no repossession risk hanging over the 16th-century coaching inn, and no conditions on materials, room count or opening dates. Savings are also immediately available without application delays or arrangement fees, letting TGI lock in heritage craftspeople before utilities (up 13.1%) and food-cost inflation climb further, and without diluting the family's sole right to manage the Grange.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development applied to TGI's financing decision and restoration.

questions.question_text: TGI is launching the 10 coach-house rooms. Consider a national food and travel magazine feature, local newspaper and radio advertising, or social media heritage-travel influencer marketing. Which should TGI choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National magazine feature: A glossy feature in a food and travel magazine would suit TGI's historic brand and reach aspirational heritage travellers nationwide. However, leads take weeks, print readership is shrinking, and the audience is untargeted — most readers will never book one inn in one county; the $18-premium coach-house rooms are better sold with moving visuals than text, and the cost competes directly with the $720,000 restoration budget.

Local newspaper and radio: Cheap and immediate, reaching the regional weekend-break market exactly where domestic weekend-break demand rose 6.1%. But reach is capped at the county, frequency depends on budget, and it cannot show the restored rooms; local residents already fill the 61% occupancy, so the 10 new premium rooms must draw guests from farther afield to pay back.

Social media heritage-travel influencer marketing: Heritage-travel creators can film the timber-framed restoration, the coach-house dining room and the $88 average room rate, reaching the 72% who choose character properties and the 65% willing to pay a premium — precisely the coach-house segment. 8.5-week diary bookings are directly trackable from links and codes, and costs are low against the build.

Recommendation: TGI should choose social media heritage-travel influencer marketing. It reaches the exact premium heritage segment at a fraction of magazine advertising cost, outruns local print in geographic reach, and turns restoration progress into a booking diary filled 8.5 weeks ahead of opening. The national magazine is rejected as unaffordable and slow for a single-site inn; local newspaper and radio are rejected as too narrow to fill 10 premium rooms — modest local PR remains useful on launch day, but not as the lead channel.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TGI with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TGI with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the magazine feature and local advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: TGI's service-quality complaints have risen to 19 per month and absenteeism is 8%. Explain two benefits for TGI of Margaret adopting a more democratic leadership style to motivate her team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership replaces laissez-faire drift with genuine consultation — staff help set service standards, menu rotas and complaint-response routines, meeting esteem needs (Maslow) and raising accountability. An innkeeper who listens reduces the inconsistency driving complaints from 12 to 19 per month, because staff own the fixes rather than waiting for instruction that may never come.

Point 2: Involvement lifts morale and retention where absenteeism has reached 8% — kitchen and waiting staff who help design pre-shift briefings and feedback loops feel respected, reducing sickness absence and the overtime it forces onto Margaret and senior staff. Democratic consultation also suits a 23-person flat structure, where the head chef and senior server directly influence the whole team's standards, cutting complaint rates without costly external quality consultants or an extra manager's salary, and giving junior members a clear, respectful route to raise concerns before they resign.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TGI's complaints, absenteeism and small-team dynamics.

questions.question_text: TGI must train 9 staff on the refurbished kitchen equipment. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the culinary college. Which should TGI choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning on the inn's own refurbished equipment during live service is directly relevant, costs nothing in course fees and keeps the 9 staff productive through the dinner rush — critical while occupancy runs at 61% and the coach-house diary opens. Coaching by the head chef builds internal craft culture. Drawbacks: mistakes affect real diners (already the source of rising complaints), bad habits spread, and no external certification is recorded for insurers or the local food hygiene authority.

Off-the-job training: The culinary college course at $650 per employee — $5,850 for 9 staff, modest against a $720,000 restoration — provides structured, certified training with a clear syllabus, an external view of TGI's kitchen routines and auditable records, directly targeting the service-consistency problem that laissez-faire leadership allowed to grow. It removes 9 staff for days, colliding with autumn wedding bookings and tightening pressure behind the 8% absenteeism rate, and the equipment curriculum may not match TGI's refurbished line exactly.

Decision: TGI should choose on-the-job training for the six junior kitchen and waiting staff, combined with one off-the-job college day for the head chef and two seniors. This protects service during the launch and the complaint recovery, costs well under $5,850, and is specific to the refurbished equipment. Full off-the-job training for all 9 is rejected because losing a third of the team to college in peak season would deepen the absenteeism problem and worsen the very complaints TGI is trying to fix; college certification can follow later for senior hires.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TGI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of TGI.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of TGI with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and service consistency.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TGI's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $150,000 ÷ ($37 − $22) = $150,000 ÷ $15 = 10,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 10,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $37 − $22 = $15.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TGI's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. TGI's management can compare the 10,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 16,000 units to confirm the restaurant is above break-even with a margin of safety of 6,000 units, informing whether coach-house launch revenue can subsidise quiet January trading.
2. Contribution per unit of $15 lets Margaret model a dinner-bed-and-breakfast coach-house bundle: a $4 add-on lifts contribution to $19 with no new fixed costs, testable against the 8.5-week diary lead time.
3. Fixed costs of $150,000 against the $450,000 bank loan help TGI check cash cover in low months, decide the loan term, and avoid breaching the $270,000 personal-savings safety buffer.
4. Unit cost data ($150,000 ÷ 16,000 units + $22 = $31.38 a unit) benchmarks the true cost per cover, guiding portion sizes, menu engineering and the viability of the $18 coach-house premium.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 10,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $15 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety (6,000 units vs 16,000 output) cushions off-peak losses; bundle pricing stacks on top of the 8.5-week diary lead time; fixed-cost cover tests the $450,000 loan against $150,000 fixed costs; and the $31.38 unit cost disciplines menu engineering, portions and the $18 coach-house premium decision for the restored wing.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TGI's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TGI's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.55 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.63 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.65 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.92 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $20,000 trade receivables + $48,000 cash = $163,000; 2025 current assets = $85,000 + $25,000 + $85,000 = $195,000. 2024 = $163,000 ÷ $105,000 = 1.55 : 1; 2025 = $195,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.63 : 1 (1.625). Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($163,000 − $95,000) ÷ $105,000 = $68,000 ÷ $105,000 = 0.65 : 1; 2025 = ($195,000 − $85,000) ÷ $120,000 = $110,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.92 : 1.

Evaluation: Liquidity improved — cash strengthened from $48,000 to $85,000 (partly coach-house deposits) and receivables stayed negligible ($20,000 to $25,000), typical of cash-and-card inn trade. Inventories eased from $95,000 to $85,000 as food purchasing tightened amid 8.8% hospitality food-cost inflation; liabilities rose modestly from $105,000 to $120,000. The inventory-excluded measure jumped from 0.65 to 0.92 — a big step, though still just below 1.00 and thin against $450,000 of bank-loan repayments and the peak $720,000 restoration spend. Non-current assets rose to $1,750,000 and capital employed to $1,970,000 as the coach-house works progressed.

Conclusion: TGI's financial position has improved on both measures; the trend is encouraging and does not depend on inventory. The residual risk is the still-below-1.00 quick measure heading into winter, when occupancy has historically dipped — Margaret should keep coach-house deposits flowing, renegotiate supplier terms and draw the loan in stages so the stronger position survives the restoration's peak cash demand.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TGI's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TGI of restoring the coach house with sustainable materials.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Sustainable restoration (reclaimed timber, natural insulation, low-VOC finishes) reinforces the 72% historic-character appeal and the $18 premium positioning, differentiating TGI from generic hotels and aligning with heritage-tourism visits growing 4.4% and domestic weekend-break demand up 6.1%, while strengthening TGI's story for press coverage and the conservation officer whose goodwill the restoration needs. Better insulation also cuts exposure to the 13.1% utilities rise, improving comfort for guests paying $88 a night while reducing the inn's running costs across all ten coach-house rooms.

Disadvantage: Specialist sustainable materials cost more and take longer to source, pushing against the $720,000 budget and the 8.5-week booking diary; delays ripple into the 10-room launch and risk opening with unfinished rooms that inflame the service-quality complaints already at 19 per month. Sustainable fittings also need careful maintenance and staff briefings for the 23-person team under laissez-faire leadership, so standards and supervision must be planned before the coach house opens.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TGI's heritage positioning, costs and restoration timeline.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 13.1% rise in utilities and energy costs will affect TGI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.8% to 5.5%): TGI's $450,000 bank loan costs about $3,150 a year more (0.7% on the loan), absorbable within $150,000 of fixed costs; however, if the restoration draws extra credit for overruns the higher rate applies to that too, and wider mortgage anxiety dampens discretionary weekend breaks.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $12.66): Kitchen, waiting and housekeeping roles sit near the minimum; senior staff are above it. If, for illustration, 12 of the 23 staff earn near the minimum, the extra $0.66 per hour costs about $15,800 a year — awkward, but partly offsettable by the coach-house premium and tighter rotas under the more democratic style Margaret is adopting.

Utilities and energy costs (+13.1%): A 16th-century coaching inn is inherently energy-hungry — heating, hot water, kitchen and laundry across a heritage shell — so 13.1% applies to the entire energy base, permanently, with no switching fix and irrespective of occupancy (which ran 54% to 61% this year). It compounds with 8.8% hospitality food-cost inflation on every restaurant cover at $88-and-under price points.

Conclusion: The 13.1% rise in utilities and energy costs will have the greatest impact. It is the largest percentage change, applies every day the inn is open, cannot be refinanced like the loan or trained away like wages, and stacks with 8.8% food inflation across 16,000 covers. The wage rise (about $15,800 a year) is second and partly offsettable through rotas and premium pricing; the interest rise costs only about $3,150 a year. TGI should invest in insulation and a heat pump within the restoration budget, audit energy suppliers, and menu-engineer to dilute 8.8% food inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TGI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TGI's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TGI with a well-justified judgement that the utilities and energy cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
